title: A time-limited reset of severe addiction

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a finite intervention after which people with a specified severe substance use disorder remain durably free of compulsive use once treatment has ended. The intervention might act biologically or through a defined brain circuit. Its defining feature would be sustained clinical benefit after a planned stop, without indefinite replacement therapy. A first convincing demonstration could concern one specified opioid, alcohol, or stimulant use disorder; success across all addictions is not required to establish this initial capability.

Conceptual clarification: “reset” names the proposed lasting change in clinical outcome. It does not establish that addiction has a single reversible mechanism or that successful treatment must restore the brain to a previous state. Sustained remission after a finite intervention could establish the clinical capability even before its causal mechanism is fully understood.

significance.text: The clinical motivation is the difficulty of sustaining benefit after treatment ends. The supplied 2015 systematic review describes buprenorphine maintenance as highly efficacious, while reporting frequent return to illicit opioid use after discontinuation. That combination makes durable benefit after a finite intervention a consequential treatment goal without diminishing the value of maintenance treatment.

Conditional significance: if a controlled trial demonstrated substantial, durable freedom from compulsive use after treatment stopped, it would establish a new capability for the tested disorder. Patients who responded could retain that benefit without continuing the intervention indefinitely. “Cure-like remission” would be a reasonable description over the observed follow-up, but a twelve-month result would establish neither permanent cure nor reversal of an underlying persistence mechanism.

Conditional downstream possibilities include extension to other drug classes and behavioral addictions while preserving normal motivation and enjoyment. These outcomes would require separate evidence and could require additional breakthroughs. A treatment that suppresses drug seeking by broadly blunting reward would have a different practical value from one that restores a satisfying life. Neither generalization nor preservation of normal reward function follows automatically from a successful result in one disorder.

missing_breakthrough.text: The capability to be established is reliable, lasting remission after a finite intervention ends in a prespecified population with severe addiction. The discontinuation evidence motivates this objective, but relapse after stopping buprenorphine does not itself identify the cause of persistence or prove that a biological reset is necessary. Treatment discontinuation outcomes alone cannot establish a universal causal barrier across substance use disorders.

Mechanistic hypotheses retained from the research include entrenched habit circuits, a drug-altered motivational set point, and learned relief from withdrawal. These are proposed explanations here, not findings evaluated by the supplied abstract. A mechanism-directed approach would need to determine which processes causally sustain compulsive use, whether different patients depend on different processes, and whether those processes can be changed durably without impairing ordinary reward and motivation. The supplied evidence does not establish that a reversible persistence mechanism remains unidentified today.

Engineering synthesis: a finite intervention would need effects that outlast its active delivery and remain useful when patients encounter drug cues, stress, withdrawal-related experiences, or renewed access to the substance. Clinical evaluation must distinguish lasting remission from short-lived suppression, continued effects of concurrent treatment, and an apparent success produced by selective follow-up. Mechanistic evidence would strengthen an explanation of how the intervention works, but the clinical endpoint and proof of a biological reset are separate achievements.

current_state.text: Bentzley and colleagues’ 2015 systematic review, “Discontinuation of buprenorphine maintenance therapy: perspectives and outcomes,” reported that relapse to illicit opioid use exceeded 50 percent in every included study at one month after discontinuation. The retained abstract also reports that patients often wanted to remain on treatment because they feared relapse. These findings concern buprenorphine discontinuation in the reviewed studies; they are not an estimated failure rate for every planned finite intervention or for severe addiction generally.

Most discontinuations described in the review were involuntary, often following failure to meet program requirements. This context limits extrapolation to a planned stop after a successful finite intervention. The review supports the clinical importance of relapse following discontinuation, but does not show that a carefully selected, prospectively treated population would have the same outcomes.

The supplied review assessed one identity-verified PubMed record containing the abstract rather than the full article. The source index reports no extraction issue or truncation for that saved record, but this does not make the underlying article fully available. The retained abstract does not describe a qualifying reset intervention, and its scope cannot establish that no such intervention exists.

Evidence boundary: no later studies or freshness searches were supplied. Consequently, the earlier assertions about later methadone and buprenorphine discontinuation outcomes, mortality benefits, and the absence of equivalent treatments for alcohol or stimulant disorders cannot be established from this evidence. The record also cannot determine whether a qualifying finite intervention exists as of November 1, 2026. These limitations leave those questions open; they do not invalidate the supported 2015 findings or show that the omitted assertions are false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: conduct a preregistered controlled trial in a prespecified population with one severe opioid, alcohol, or stimulant use disorder. Deliver a time-limited biological or circuit intervention, followed by a planned stop, and assess outcomes twelve months after treatment ends. A proposed clinical bar is that a majority of the treated severe group remains free of compulsive use, with a substantial advantage over controls. The original aspiration that success be common in the treated arm and rare in controls should be expressed through prespecified absolute rates and between-group differences. Neither twelve months nor the majority threshold is an established standard supplied by the source.
completion_criteria.label: Majority avoid compulsive use twelve months post-treatment, substantially outperforming controls

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement requirements: define abstinence and any permitted non-compulsive use before enrollment, including how loss of control and harmful consequences will be assessed. Use prespecified confirmation methods, follow-up procedures, handling of missing outcomes, and rules for concurrent treatments. Monitor mortality, use of other substances, and return to treatment so that loss to follow-up or substitution of another substance does not create a misleading impression of remission. Continued agonist maintenance would not satisfy this concept’s finite-treatment endpoint, although it remains a distinct therapeutic option.
completion_criteria.label: Prespecified remission criteria and monitoring account for attrition and substitution

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: seek independent replication and report outcomes across relevant patient groups, clinical settings, and concurrent care. Assess adverse effects, normal reward function, motivation, and quality of life alongside substance-use outcomes. Freedom from anhedonia is an important later property rather than a required component of the first efficacy demonstration, but adverse effects still determine whether that demonstration is clinically useful. Longer follow-up would test durability beyond twelve months. Finite trials establish demonstrated breadth within their populations and conditions; they cannot establish permanent cure or literal universality across addictions.
completion_criteria.label: Report independent replication efforts, clinical outcomes, and demonstrated treatment limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based distinction: PSY-08, “Selective and durable modification of a pathological memory,” could overlap if changing drug-related memories or cues helped sustain remission. Weakening one cue alone would not establish PSY-09 unless it produced the broader durable clinical outcome after treatment ended. PSY-08’s supplied title concerns pathological memory generally; treating cue-specific weakening as one possible application avoids narrowing that separate concept without evidence.

Roster-based distinction: PSY-07, “Reliable causal control of a core symptom by a defined circuit,” could provide an intervention route, but causal control during stimulation would not by itself demonstrate lasting freedom from compulsive use after stimulation stops. PSY-10, “Reopening plasticity that can repair an established psychiatric deficit,” could provide another route to durable change. PSY-09 is defined by the addiction outcome and finite treatment course rather than by circuit control or plasticity as its required mechanism.

Roster-based distinction: PSY-01, “Mechanism-defined diseases in place of the major syndromes,” and PSY-05, “Medicines designed from a confirmed human disease mechanism,” could help identify causal subgroups or develop targeted treatments. PSY-09 does not require that all severe addiction share one mechanism, nor would clinical remission alone confirm a mechanism. PSY-06, “A clinical instrument that reads an individual’s psychiatric state,” could assist measurement or patient selection, but measurement capability is separate from producing remission.

Roster-based distinction: PSY-02, “A treatment that changes the course of schizophrenia,” and PSY-03, “Ending the relapsing course of severe mood disorders,” share the ambition of changing a disorder’s longer-term course. PSY-09 adds a specific requirement that benefit persist after a finite addiction intervention ends. These are separate disorder-specific achievements; success in one would not establish success in another.

Roster-based distinction: PSY-04, “Primary prevention that lowers incidence of a major disorder,” and PSY-11, “Prevention of post-traumatic stress disorder by blocking consolidation,” concern prevention, whereas PSY-09 targets established severe addiction. PSY-12, “A session-level amplifier that lets brief psychotherapy match a full course,” shares an interest in limited treatment burden, but matching a psychotherapy course does not itself establish durable post-treatment remission from severe addiction.

change_log.change: Preserved PSY-09 and its title while defining “reset” through durable clinical outcomes after finite treatment.
change_log.reason: The concept remains coherent without assuming that one reversible biological mechanism has been identified.

change_log.change: Retained habit circuits, altered motivation, and learned withdrawal relief as explicitly labeled hypotheses.
change_log.reason: They provide useful explanatory possibilities, but the supplied abstract does not evaluate them or establish the current limits of mechanistic knowledge.

change_log.change: Preserved the 2015 one-month relapse figure and added the predominance of involuntary discontinuations.
change_log.reason: The quantitative finding is supported, while discontinuation circumstances limit comparison with a planned stop after a finite intervention.

change_log.change: Replaced unsupported present-day treatment and mortality assertions with explicit evidence boundaries.
change_log.reason: No later studies or freshness searches were supplied, so neither those assertions nor a comprehensive absence of qualifying interventions can be established.

change_log.change: Limited cure-like language to observed follow-up and separated clinical success from mechanistic reversal.
change_log.reason: Durable remission over a measured interval does not prove permanent cure or a biological reset.

change_log.change: Preserved cross-addiction generalization and normal reward function as conditional further achievements.
change_log.reason: They require separate evidence and may require additional breakthroughs rather than following automatically from one discovery.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed demonstration with endpoint definitions, missing-outcome handling, concurrent-treatment rules, safety assessment, and independent replication.
change_log.reason: These distinctions make the finite-treatment claim interpretable without presenting proposed thresholds as established standards.

change_log.change: Qualified the PSY-08 cue-memory comparison and explained relationships to the supplied roster.
change_log.reason: The roster supports conceptual comparisons, but does not establish detailed boundaries or justify merging separate innovations.

change_log.change: Preserved the distinction between a successfully extracted PubMed record and access to the full article.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence review was based on a partial article record despite the absence of extraction problems.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence cannot determine whether a qualifying finite intervention exists as of November 1, 2026.
The full article was not available in the supplied review, leaving study-level populations, methods, and outcomes beyond the retained abstract unassessed.
The causal roles and reversibility of the proposed persistence mechanisms remain unestablished by the supplied material.
The proposed twelve-month duration, majority threshold, control comparison, and definition of non-compulsive use require disorder-specific operational choices and justification.
Generalization across substances, behavioral addictions, and patient groups, as well as preservation of normal reward function, would require separate demonstrations.
Later mortality and discontinuation findings and treatment availability across alcohol and stimulant disorders remain unassessed rather than disproven.

brief.title: Lasting freedom from addiction after treatment ends
possible: People with severe addiction could finish a planned course of treatment and remain free of drug or alcohol use they cannot control. A treatment acting on the body or brain could leave a lasting benefit after it stops.
why: People who respond could keep the benefit without continuing treatment indefinitely. This would address a central difficulty in addiction care, sustaining recovery after treatment ends.

sources.showed: Their review found frequent return to illicit opioid use after people stopped buprenorphine, a medicine used to treat opioid addiction. Most stopped involuntarily, often because of program requirements.
sources.quote: Patients often desired to remain on BMT because of fear of relapse to illicit opioid use if they were to discontinue BMT.
sources.cited_for: The review shows why sustaining recovery after treatment ends matters.
sources.not_established: Stopping an effective ongoing medicine does not test lasting recovery after a treatment designed to end.

sources.showed: A trial tested long-acting naltrexone, a medicine for opioid addiction, in people involved with the criminal justice system. After treatment ended, the groups had equal rates of urine samples free of opioids.
sources.cited_for: The trial illustrates the need to measure outcomes after treatment ends and track other treatments and adverse effects.
sources.not_established: The trial did not demonstrate a lasting advantage after treatment stopped.

sources.who: Patrick Bach and colleagues, including the DeBraSTRA study group
sources.showed: A trial in 12 people tested deep brain stimulation, electrical pulses delivered through implanted electrodes, for severe alcohol addiction. Some drinking measures improved during stimulation. The main test of continuous abstinence, avoiding alcohol entirely, was inconclusive.
sources.quote:
The primary intention-to-treat analysis, comparing continuous
abstinence between treatment groups, did not yield statistically signi ﬁcant results, most likely due to the restricted number of
participants.
sources.cited_for: The trial supports further testing of brain stimulation for alcohol addiction.
sources.not_established: The small trial did not establish continuous abstinence or lasting recovery after stimulation stopped.

shown: Bach and colleagues found more alcohol-free days during active brain stimulation in a small controlled trial. Its main test of continuous abstinence was inconclusive. Lee and colleagues found equal opioid-free urine results between groups after a medicine course ended.
missing: A controlled trial would need to establish lasting freedom from compulsive use after a planned treatment stop in a defined severe addiction.
Outcome tracking would need to account for missing participants, other treatments, deaths and switching substances.
Independent teams would need to reproduce the benefit and establish its safety and limits.

milestones.label: Most patients avoid compulsive use a year after treatment
milestones.explanation: A controlled trial would have to show that most treated patients avoid compulsive use twelve months after stopping, substantially outperforming controls. This would establish lasting benefit for the tested severe addiction.

milestones.label: Recovery measures account for missing follow-up and substance switching
milestones.explanation: Rules set in advance would have to define recovery and track missing outcomes, deaths, substance switching and other treatments. This would make apparent recovery a credible measure of lasting freedom from compulsive use.

milestones.label: Independent replication establishes benefits and treatment limits
milestones.explanation: Independent studies would have to report replication efforts, outcomes across patients and settings, harms, enjoyment, motivation and quality of life. Longer follow-up would test durability and clarify clinical usefulness.

uncertain: The proposed follow-up duration, success threshold and permitted substance use need justification for each addiction.
Whether lasting recovery requires reversing a particular biological process remains open.
Benefits across other addictions, and preservation of ordinary enjoyment and motivation, require separate demonstrations.
